name: Python
description: Python is a beginner-friendly language with clean syntax, used for web back-ends, automation, data science and AI.

blocks.html:
Introduction to Python

What is Python?

Python is a popular, beginner-friendly programming language. Its code reads almost like English, which is why it is used for web back-ends, data science, automation, AI and teaching. It was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991.

  • Interpreted: you run code line by line, no separate compile step.
  • Dynamically typed: you do not declare types.
  • Batteries included: a huge standard library comes with it.
  • Readable: indentation and simple words make programs easy to follow.
  • Multi-purpose: supports procedural, object-oriented and functional styles.
  • Free and open source: works on Windows, macOS and Linux.

Where Python Is Used

AreaWhat you can buildPopular tools
Web developmentWebsites, REST APIs, dashboardsDjango, Flask, FastAPI
Data scienceCleaning, analysing and charting datapandas, NumPy, Matplotlib
AI and machine learningPrediction models, computer vision, chatbotsscikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, OpenCV
AutomationRenaming files, sending emails, scraping websitesos, shutil, requests, Selenium
Games and appsSimple 2D games and desktop toolspygame, Tkinter
Testing and DevOpsTest scripts and server toolspytest, Fabric, Ansible

Installing and Running Python

Download Python from python.org. On Windows, tick Add Python to PATH in the installer. Then open a terminal (Command Prompt, PowerShell or Terminal) and check the version:

python --version
# On macOS / Linux you may need:
python3 --version

There are three common ways to run Python code:

WayHowBest for
Interactive prompt (REPL)Type python, then write one line at a time. Type exit() to leave.Trying small ideas quickly
Script fileSave code in hello.py and run python hello.pyReal programs
Editor or notebookVS Code, PyCharm, IDLE or Jupyter NotebookDaily work, debugging, data analysis

Your First Program

Save this as hello.py and run it with python hello.py (or try it in the interactive prompt by typing python).

blocks.code:
# My first Python program
print("Hello, Learning Hub!")
print(2 + 3)
print("Python", "is", "fun")
blocks.output:
Hello, Learning Hub!
5
Python is fun

blocks.html:
• print() shows text on the screen.
  • # starts a comment: Python ignores the rest of the line.
  • Text goes in quotes (single or double).
print(), Comments and Escape Characters

blocks.code:
# Comments explain your code to humans
name = "Sara"
print("Hello", name)                 # items are separated by a space
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")        # change the separator
print("Loading", end="...")          # change what comes at the end
print("done")
print("Tab\there", "New\nline")      # \t is a tab, \n is a new line
print("She said \"hi\"")             # escape a quote with a backslash
print('It\'s fine')
print("Total:", 10 + 5)
print(5 + 3, 5 - 3, 5 * 3, 5 / 3)
blocks.output:
Hello Sara
a-b-c
Loading...done
Tab	here New
line
She said "hi"
It's fine
Total: 15
8 2 15 1.6666666666666667

blocks.html:
EscapeMeaning
\nNew line
\tTab
\\One backslash
\"A double quote inside double quotes

blocks.code:
"""A triple-quoted text can span many lines.
It is also used for docstrings, which describe a file,
a function or a class."""
print("Comments use #, docstrings use triple quotes")
blocks.output: Comments use #, docstrings use triple quotes

blocks.html: Good comments explain why you did something, not what the code obviously does. Keep them short and up to date.

Indentation Is Part of the Syntax

Other languages use { } to group code. Python uses indentation (4 spaces is the standard). Code with the wrong indentation is an error.

blocks.code:
age = 20
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")      # indented: inside the if
    print("Can vote")
print("Done")           # not indented: always runs

blocks.html: The colon : at the end of a line opens a block, and the indented lines below it belong to that block.

Why Learn Python First?

StrengthExample
Short codeA task that takes 10 lines in Java is often 3 in Python
Huge communityLibraries for web (Django, Flask), data (pandas) and AI (PyTorch)
Great for learningYou focus on ideas, not on syntax noise
Good jobsPython is asked for in data, AI, automation and back-end roles

Common Beginner Errors

Errors are normal. Read the last line of the error message first: it names the problem and Python shows the line number.

ErrorExampleUsual cause and fix
SyntaxErrorprint("Hi"A missing bracket, quote or colon. Check the line shown.
IndentationErrorA line is not aligned with the lines aboveUse 4 spaces everywhere and never mix tabs and spaces.
NameErrorprint(nme)A name was misspelled or used before it was created.
TypeError"5" + 3You mixed incompatible types. Convert with int() or str().
ZeroDivisionError10 / 0Dividing by zero is not allowed.

Practice Time

  1. Print your name, your roll number and your favourite language on three separate lines.
  2. Print the result of 12 * 7 + 5 and of 100 / 8.
  3. Use sep and end so that print("2026", "11", "20") shows 2026/11/20.
  4. Write a comment above every line of a program that prints a small rectangle of * characters.
  5. Break a working program on purpose (remove a bracket) and read the error message.

Quick Summary

  • Python is an interpreted, readable, general-purpose language.
  • Programs run from a .py file with python file.py, or line by line in the REPL.
  • print() displays output; # makes a comment.
  • Indentation is part of the syntax: use 4 spaces.
  • Error messages are helpful: read the last line and the line number.

Variables, Types & Input

Variables

A variable is a name for a value. You create it by assigning with =. There is no type to write: Python works it out.

blocks.code:
name = "Ayesha"
age = 20
height = 1.62
is_student = True

print(name, age, height, is_student)

age = age + 1          # variables can change
print(age)

blocks.html:
• Names use letters, digits and underscores, and cannot start with a digit.
  • Python style is snake_case (student_name).
  • Names are case sensitive: age and Age are different.
  • You cannot use keywords such as if, for, class or True as names.
  • Choose meaningful names: total_marks is better than tm.
Multiple Assignment and Swapping

blocks.code:
a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
x = y = 0
print(a, b, c, x, y)

a, b = b, a            # swap without a temporary variable
print(a, b)

first, *rest = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(first, rest)

blocks.html: By convention, a name written in capitals such as PI = 3.14159 or MAX_USERS = 50 is a constant. Python does not stop you from changing it, but other programmers will expect you not to.

Variables Are Names, Not Boxes

A variable does not hold the value inside it; it points to a value. This matters when two names point to the same changeable value.

blocks.code:
x = 5
y = x
y = y + 1
print(x, y)           # ints cannot change, so x is untouched

a = [1, 2]
b = a                 # both names point to the SAME list
b.append(3)
print(a, b, a is b)

blocks.html: You will see this again in Lists and Functions. Remember: = between two names never copies a list.

Basic Types

TypeExampleMeaning
int42Whole numbers (any size)
float3.14Decimal numbers
str"hello"Text
boolTrue / FalseYes or no
NoneTypeNoneMeans "no value"

Use type(x) to see the type, and int(), float(), str() to convert between types.

blocks.code:
x = 7
print(type(x))
print(type(7.0))
print(type("7"))
print(type(True))
print(int("5") + 3)      # text -> number
print(str(5) + "3")      # number -> text
print(float(2))

blocks.html: Numbers in Depth

blocks.code:
print(2 ** 100)                 # integers never overflow
print(1_000_000 + 1)            # underscores make big numbers readable
print(0.1 + 0.2)                # floats are approximate
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))
print(abs(-7.5), round(3.14159, 2), pow(2, 5))
print(divmod(17, 5))            # (quotient, remainder)
print(10 / 4, 10 // 4, -10 // 4)
print(int(3.9), int(-3.9), round(2.5), round(3.5))
print(3 + 4j)                   # complex numbers exist too

blocks.html:
• Floats store approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Use round() when you show results.
  • int() cuts off the decimal part; round() rounds (and rounds halves to the nearest even number).
  • // is floor division: it rounds down, so -10 // 4 is -3.
Booleans and None

blocks.code:
print(bool(0), bool(5), bool(""), bool("a"), bool([]), bool(None))
print(True + True, int(False))
result = None
print(result, result is None)
print(10 > 3, 10 == 3, 10 != 3)
blocks.output:
False True False True False False
2 0
None True
True False True

blocks.html: None is used when a value is missing or a function has nothing to return. Compare it with is None.

f-strings and Input

An f-string puts values inside text: write f"..." and put variables in { }. To read from the keyboard use input(), which always gives text, so convert it when you need a number.

blocks.code:
name = "Sara"
score = 87.456
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f}%")
print(f"Double: {score * 2:.2f}")
print(f"{name.upper()} has {len(name)} letters")
blocks.output:
Sara scored 87.5%
Double: 174.91
SARA has 4 letters

blocks.html:
name = input("Your name: ")
age = int(input("Your age: "))      # convert text to a number
print(f"Hello {name}, next year you will be {age + 1}")
Formatting Output Nicely

blocks.code:
price = 1234.5
ratio = 0.256
name = "Sara"
print(f"{price:,.2f}")                       # thousands separator, 2 decimals
print(f"{ratio:.1%}")                        # percentage
print(f"|{name:>8}|{name:<8}|{name:^8}|")    # right, left, centre
print(f"{5:03d}")                            # zero padding
x = 7
print(f"{x = }")                             # handy for debugging

blocks.html:
FormatMeaningExample result
:.2f2 decimal places3.14
:,thousands separator1,000,000
:.1%percentage with 1 decimal25.6%
:>8right-align in 8 characters Sara
:03dpad with zeros to width 3007
Mini Project: Unit Converter

blocks.code:
celsius = 36.6
fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
print(f"{celsius} C = {fahrenheit:.1f} F")

km = 12.5
print(f"{km} km = {km * 0.621371:.2f} miles")

radius = 7
area = 3.14159 * radius ** 2
print(f"Circle of radius {radius}: area = {area:.2f}")
blocks.output:
36.6 C = 97.9 F
12.5 km = 7.77 miles
Circle of radius 7: area = 153.94

blocks.html:
Now make it interactive with input(). Remember to convert the text to a number first:

celsius = float(input("Temperature in C: "))
print(f"{celsius * 9 / 5 + 32:.1f} F")

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting that input() returns text: "5" + "3" is "53", not 8.
  • Using = when you mean == (assign versus compare).
  • Using a name before giving it a value (NameError).
  • Naming a variable list, str or print, which hides the built-in with the same name.
  • Expecting 0.1 + 0.2 to equal 0.3 exactly.

Practice Time

  1. Store your name, age and city in variables and print one sentence with an f-string.
  2. Swap the values of two variables without a third variable.
  3. Ask for two numbers and print their sum, difference, product and average (2 decimals).
  4. Convert 5000 seconds into hours, minutes and seconds using // and %.
  5. Ask for a price and a discount percentage and print the final price.

Quick Summary

  • A variable is a name pointing to a value; no type is declared.
  • Main types: int, float, str, bool, None.
  • type() shows a type; int(), float(), str() convert.
  • input() always returns text.
  • f-strings with format codes make clean output.

Operators & Conditions

Operators

KindOperatorsNotes
Arithmetic+ - * // always gives a float
More arithmetic// % **floor division, remainder, power
Comparison== != < > <= >=give True or False
Logicaland or notcombine conditions
Membershipin not inis something inside a list or text?
Identityis is notare two names the same object?

blocks.code:
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ** 10)
print(5 > 3, 5 == 5.0, "a" < "b")
print(True and False, True or False, not True)
print("py" in "python", 3 in [1, 2, 3])
blocks.output:
3.5 3 1 1024
True True True
False True False
True True

blocks.html: Assignment Operators and Precedence

blocks.code:
n = 10
n += 5; print(n)       # n = n + 5
n -= 3; print(n)
n *= 2; print(n)
n //= 5; print(n)
n **= 2; print(n)
n %= 7; print(n)

print(2 + 3 * 4, (2 + 3) * 4, -2 ** 2, (-2) ** 2)
print(not 5 > 3 or 2 < 1)

blocks.html:
Order (high to low)Operators
1( ) brackets
2** power
3unary -x
4* / // %
5+ -
6comparisons: < > == != in is
7not, then and, then or

When in doubt, use brackets. They make code easier to read as well as correct.
Chained Comparisons, == and is

blocks.code:
age = 25
print(18 <= age < 30)         # chained comparison, reads like maths

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b, a is c)   # same value vs same object

value = None
print(value is None)

blocks.html:
• == asks: do they have the same value?
  • is asks: are they the very same object? Use it for None: x is None.
  • Never compare text or numbers with is; use ==.

if, elif, else

Conditions let your program choose. Python checks from top to bottom and runs only the first matching block.

• Do not forget the colon and the indentation.
  • Use == to compare and = to assign.
  • elif means "else if" (you can have many).
Nested if and the One-Line if
If a block must exist but has nothing to do yet, write pass. It is a placeholder that does nothing.

Truthiness

Python treats some values as False in a condition: 0, 0.0, "", [], {} and None. Everything else is True.

blocks.code:
for value in [0, 1, "", "hi", [], [0], None]:
    print(repr(value), "->", "True" if value else "False")
blocks.output:
0 -> False
1 -> True
'' -> False
'hi' -> True
[] -> False
[0] -> True
None -> False

blocks.html: and, or, not and Short-Circuiting

blocks.code:
x = 0
print(x != 0 and 10 / x > 1)      # safe: the division never runs
print(x == 0 or 10 / x > 1)       # also skipped

name = ""
display = name or "Guest"         # or gives the first truthy value
print(display)

print(any([False, 0, "x"]), all([1, "a", True]), all([]))
blocks.output:
False
True
Guest
True True True

blocks.html:
• a and b stops at the first False; a or b stops at the first True.
  • any() is True if at least one item is truthy; all() is True if every item is truthy.

match and case (Python 3.10+)

match compares one value against several patterns. It is a cleaner version of a long elif chain.

blocks.code:
code = 404
match code:
    case 200:
        print("OK")
    case 404:
        print("Not found")
    case 500 | 503:
        print("Server problem")
    case _:
        print("Unknown")

blocks.html: case _ is the default: it matches anything not matched above.
Small Programs

blocks.code:
year = 2024
is_leap = (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0) or year % 400 == 0
print(year, "leap year?", is_leap)

n = 17
print(n, "is", "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd")
print("Divisible by 3 and 5?", n % 3 == 0 and n % 5 == 0)

a, b, c = 7, 3, 9
print("Largest:", max(a, b, c))

username, password = "admin", "1234"
if username == "admin" and password == "1234":
    print("Login successful")
else:
    print("Wrong username or password")
blocks.output:
2024 leap year? True
17 is odd
Divisible by 3 and 5? False
Largest: 9
Login successful

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Writing if x = 5: instead of if x == 5:.
  • Forgetting the colon or the indentation after if, elif, else.
  • Writing if x == 1 or 2: (always true). Write if x == 1 or x == 2: or if x in (1, 2):.
  • Comparing text without thinking about case: "Yes" == "yes" is False. Use .lower().
  • Using is to compare numbers or strings.

Practice Time

  1. Ask for a number and say whether it is positive, negative or zero.
  2. Ask for marks (0-100) and print the grade with if / elif / else.
  3. Ask for three numbers and print the largest without using max().
  4. Ask for a year and tell whether it is a leap year.
  5. Ask for a day number 1-7 and print the day name using match.

Quick Summary

  • Comparison operators give True or False; combine them with and, or, not.
  • Use elif for more choices and else for the rest.
  • == compares values; is compares identity (use it for None).
  • Empty values (0, "", [], {}, None) are False in conditions.
  • match is a tidy alternative to long elif chains.

Loops

for Loops and range()

A for loop repeats code for each item in a sequence. range(n) gives the numbers 0 to n-1.

blocks.output:
Round 0
Round 1
Round 2
P
y
Sum 1..5 = 15

blocks.html:
CallGives
range(5)0, 1, 2, 3, 4
range(2, 6)2, 3, 4, 5
range(0, 10, 3)0, 3, 6, 9
range(5, 0, -1)5, 4, 3, 2, 1

while Loops

A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is True. Make sure something inside changes the condition, or the loop never ends.

blocks.code:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print("Countdown", count)
    count -= 1
print("Liftoff!")

blocks.html: Use for when you know how many times (or what items) to loop over. Use while when you loop until something happens.

break, continue and enumerate

  • break leaves the loop immediately.
  • continue skips to the next round.
  • enumerate(items) gives the index and the item together.
Looping Over Data

blocks.code:
names = ["Ali", "Sara", "Bilal"]
marks = [78, 92, 65]
for name, mark in zip(names, marks):      # two lists side by side
    print(name, mark)

for n in reversed(range(1, 4)):
    print(n, end=" ")
print()

for key, value in {"a": 1, "b": 2}.items():
    print(key, value)

print(sorted(marks, reverse=True), sum(marks), max(marks), min(marks))

blocks.html:
Nested Loops and Patterns

A loop inside a loop runs the inner loop completely for every round of the outer loop. Great for tables and patterns.

The else Part of a Loop

The else block of a loop runs only when the loop finished without hitting break. It is handy for searching.

Accumulator Patterns

Many loops follow one idea: start with an initial value, update it on every round, and use the final result.

blocks.code:
numbers = [4, 9, 2, 15, 7]
total, count, biggest = 0, 0, numbers[0]
for n in numbers:
    total += n
    count += 1
    if n > biggest:
        biggest = n
print("Sum", total, "Average", total / count, "Max", biggest)

fact = 1
for n in range(1, 6):
    fact *= n
print("5! =", fact)

a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(8):        # _ means "I do not need this variable"
    print(a, end=" ")
    a, b = b, a + b
print()

blocks.html:
while True and Input Validation

Use while True with break when you must ask again until the input is valid:

password = ""
while password != "python123":
    password = input("Enter password: ")
print("Access granted")

blocks.code:
attempts = ["abc", "12345", "python123"]    # pretend these were typed
index = 0
password = ""
while password != "python123":
    password = attempts[index]
    index += 1
    print("Tried:", password)
print("Access granted after", index, "attempts")

count = 0
while True:
    count += 1
    if count == 3:
        break
print("stopped at", count)
blocks.output:
Tried: abc
Tried: 12345
Tried: python123
Access granted after 3 attempts
stopped at 3

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to change the variable in a while loop: it runs forever (press Ctrl + C to stop it).
  • Off-by-one errors: range(5) stops at 4, and range(1, 5) stops at 4 too.
  • Changing a list while looping over it. Loop over a copy: for x in items[:]:.
  • Using range(len(items)) when you can loop directly over items.
  • Wrong indentation: a line inside the loop must be indented.

Practice Time

  1. Print the multiplication table of a number typed by the user.
  2. Print all even numbers from 1 to 50 and their sum.
  3. Print this pattern for n = 5: *, **, ***, ****, ***** (one row per line).
  4. Count the vowels in a sentence using a for loop.
  5. Ask the user for numbers until they type 0, then print the total and the average.

Quick Summary

  • for loops over items; range() makes number sequences.
  • while repeats while a condition stays True.
  • break stops a loop, continue skips a round, loop else runs if no break happened.
  • enumerate() gives index + item; zip() walks two lists together.
  • Nested loops build tables and patterns.

Strings & Text Handling

Creating Strings

A string (str) is text inside quotes. Single or double quotes both work. Triple quotes allow many lines.

blocks.code:
a = 'single'
b = "double"
c = """Triple quotes
can span lines"""
print(a, b)
print(c)
print("Line1\nLine2\tTabbed")
print(r"C:\new_folder\test")     # raw string: backslashes stay as they are
print("ha" * 3, "Py" + "thon", len("Python"))
blocks.output:
single double
Triple quotes
can span lines
Line1
Line2	Tabbed
C:\new_folder\test
hahaha Python 6

blocks.html:
Indexing and Slicing

Each character has a position (index) starting at 0. Negative indexes count from the end. A slice text[start:stop:step] takes a part (stop is not included).

blocks.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[0], word[-1], word[2])
print(word[0:2], word[2:], word[:3], word[::-1], word[::2])
for ch in "abc":
    print(ch, end=" ")
print()
print("th" in word.lower(), "z" in word)
blocks.output:
P n t
Py thon Pyt nohtyP Pto
a b c 
True False

blocks.html:
SliceResult for "Python"
word[0]P
word[-1]n
word[1:4]yth
word[:2]Py
word[::-1]nohtyP (reversed)

Strings Cannot Be Changed

Strings are immutable: you cannot change a character in place. Instead you build a new string.

blocks.code:
s = "hello"
try:
    s[0] = "H"
except TypeError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

s = "H" + s[1:]          # build a new string instead
print(s)
print("hello".capitalize())
blocks.output:
Error: 'str' object does not support item assignment
Hello
Hello

blocks.html: Useful String Methods

blocks.code:
text = "  Learning Python Is Fun  "
print(text.strip())
print(text.lower().strip(), "|", text.upper().strip())
print(text.strip().title(), "|", text.strip().swapcase())
print(text.replace("Fun", "Great").strip())
print(text.count("n"), text.find("Python"), text.find("Java"))
print("python".startswith("py"), "file.txt".endswith(".txt"))
print("abc123".isalnum(), "123".isdigit(), "abc".isalpha(), "  ".isspace())
blocks.output:
Learning Python Is Fun
learning python is fun | LEARNING PYTHON IS FUN
Learning Python Is Fun | lEARNING pYTHON iS fUN
Learning Python Is Great
4 11 -1
True True
True True True True

blocks.html:
MethodWhat it does
strip()Remove spaces (or given characters) from both ends
lower() / upper() / title()Change the case
replace(old, new)Replace every old part with new
find(x)Index of the first x, or -1 if missing
count(x)How many times x appears
startswith() / endswith()Check the beginning or end
isdigit() / isalpha() / isalnum()Check what kind of characters it contains

split() and join()

split() breaks text into a list; join() glues a list back into text. They are used all the time when reading data.

blocks.code:
sentence = "red,green,blue"
colors = sentence.split(",")
print(colors, len(colors))
print(" ".join(["Learning", "Hub"]), "-".join(colors))
print("one two  three".split())          # no argument: split on any spaces
print("line1\nline2".splitlines())
print("Hello".center(11, "*"), "7".zfill(3))

blocks.html: Formatting Strings

blocks.code:
name, score = "Ali", 91.456
print(f"{name} got {score:.1f}")                 # f-string (best choice)
print("{} got {:.1f}".format(name, score))       # older style
print("%s got %.1f" % (name, score))             # oldest style
print("Ali" + " " + str(91))                     # concatenation needs str()
blocks.output:
Ali got 91.5
Ali got 91.5
Ali got 91.5
Ali 91

blocks.html: Use f-strings in new code. They are the shortest and the easiest to read.
Small Text Programs

blocks.code:
text = "Madam"
cleaned = text.lower()
print(text, "palindrome?", cleaned == cleaned[::-1])

sentence = "Learning Python is fun"
vowels = 0
for ch in sentence.lower():
    if ch in "aeiou":
        vowels += 1
print("Vowels:", vowels)

words = sentence.split()
print(len(words), "words; longest:", max(words, key=len))
print(" ".join(word.capitalize() for word in words))

email = "student@lgu.edu.pk"
print(email.split("@")[1], email.endswith(".pk"))
blocks.output:
Madam palindrome? True
Vowels: 6
4 words; longest: Learning
Learning Python Is Fun
lgu.edu.pk True

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Trying to change a character with text[0] = "X" (strings are immutable).
  • Joining text and numbers with +: "Age: " + 20 is an error. Use an f-string or str(20).
  • Forgetting that methods return a new string: text.upper() alone does not change text. Write text = text.upper().
  • Comparing without thinking about case or spaces. Clean first with strip() and lower().

Practice Time

  1. Ask for a name and print it in reverse, in capitals and its length.
  2. Count how many times the letter a appears in a sentence.
  3. Ask for a sentence and print the number of words.
  4. Check whether a word typed by the user is a palindrome.
  5. Turn "learning hub python" into "Learning-Hub-Python" using split, title and join.

Quick Summary

  • Strings are immutable sequences of characters; slice them with [start:stop:step].
  • Common methods: strip, lower, upper, replace, find, split, join.
  • f-strings are the best way to format output.
  • Methods give back a new string; they never change the old one.

Lists & Tuples

Lists

A list holds many values in order. It is mutable: you can add, remove and change items. Indexing starts at 0 and negative indexes count from the end.

blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "mango"]
fruits.append("kiwi")
fruits.insert(0, "banana")
print(fruits)
print(fruits[0], fruits[-1], len(fruits))
fruits.remove("mango")
last = fruits.pop()
print(last, fruits)
fruits[0] = "grape"
print(sorted(fruits))

MethodWhat it does
append(x)Add to the end
insert(i, x)Add at a position
extend(list)Add all items of another list
remove(x)Remove the first x
pop()Remove and return the last item (or pop(i))
index(x) / count(x)Position of x / how many x
sort() / reverse()Sort or reverse in place
len(list)How many items
More List Operations

blocks.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums.extend([5, 4])
print(nums, nums.index(2), nums.count(3))
nums.reverse()
print(nums)
nums.sort()
print(nums)
print(nums.pop(0))
print(nums)
print(3 in nums, 99 in nums)
print(nums + [0], [0] * 3)
del nums[0]
print(nums)

blocks.html:
Slicing and Comprehensions

A slice items[start:stop] takes part of a list (stop is not included). A list comprehension builds a new list in one line.

blocks.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:4])      # index 1 to 3
print(nums[:2], nums[3:])
print(nums[::-1])     # reversed

squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
big = [n for n in nums if n > 25]
print(squares, big)

blocks.html:
Copying Lists: Alias or Copy?

b = a does not copy a list; both names point to the same list. Use .copy(), list(a) or a[:] for a copy. For lists inside lists use copy.deepcopy.

blocks.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a            # alias: same list
c = a.copy()     # real copy (also a[:] or list(a))
a.append(4)
print(a, b, c)

import copy
nested = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = nested.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(nested)
nested[0].append(99)
print(shallow[0], deep[0])   # shallow copy shares the inner lists

Sorting

blocks.code:
words = ["banana", "kiwi", "apple", "fig"]
print(sorted(words))
print(sorted(words, key=len))                 # sort by length
print(sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True))

people = [("Ali", 22), ("Sara", 19), ("Bilal", 25)]
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])               # sort by age (lambda: see Functions)
print(people)

Handy Built-ins for Lists

scores = [70, 85, 90, 65]
print(len(scores), sum(scores), min(scores), max(scores))
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))
print(any(s > 89 for s in scores), all(s >= 65 for s in scores))
print(list(range(5)), list("abc"), list(zip([1, 2], ["a", "b"])))

Tuples

A tuple is like a list that cannot change (immutable). Use it for fixed groups such as coordinates. You can unpack it into variables.

blocks.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point               # unpacking
print(x, y, point[0])

try:
    point[0] = 9
except TypeError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

print(len((1, 2, 3)), (1, 2) + (3,))

single = (5,)              # the comma makes a tuple
not_tuple = (5)
print(type(single), type(not_tuple))
t = (1, 2, 2, 3)
print(t.count(2), t.index(3), max(t), list(t))

Common Mistakes

  • Index out of range: a list of 3 items has indexes 0, 1, 2 (IndexError for 3).
  • Writing b = a and expecting a copy.
  • Writing nums = nums.sort(): sort() returns None, so nums becomes None.
  • Writing (5) and expecting a tuple: you need (5,).
  • Removing items from a list while looping over it.

Practice Time

  1. Store 5 marks in a list and print the total, average, highest and lowest.
  2. Remove duplicates from [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3] while keeping the order.
  3. Ask for names until the user types stop, then print the list sorted.
  4. Make a list of the squares of all odd numbers from 1 to 15 with a comprehension.
  5. Rotate a list by one position: [1, 2, 3, 4] becomes [2, 3, 4, 1].

Quick Summary

  • Lists are ordered and changeable; tuples are ordered and fixed.
  • Index from 0, negative indexes count from the end, slices take parts.
  • append, insert, extend, remove, pop, sort are the key methods.
  • b = a shares the list; use .copy() to copy.
  • Comprehensions build lists in one line.

Dictionaries & Sets

Dictionaries

A dictionary stores key: value pairs and finds a value quickly by its key. Keys must be unique.

blocks.code:
student = {"name": "Ali", "age": 20}
student["city"] = "Lahore"          # add
student["age"] = 21                 # change
print(student)
print(student["name"], student.get("phone", "no phone"))

for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, "=", value)

del student["city"]
print("city" in student, len(student))
blocks.output:
{'name': 'Ali', 'age': 21, 'city': 'Lahore'}
Ali no phone
name = Ali
age = 21
city = Lahore
False 2

blocks.html:
• d[key] raises an error if the key is missing; d.get(key, default) does not.
  • d.items() gives (key, value) pairs for looping.
  • key in d checks if a key exists.
Dictionary Methods

blocks.code:
d = {"name": "Ali", "age": 20}
print(list(d.keys()), list(d.values()))
d.update({"age": 21, "city": "Lahore"})
print(d)
print(d.pop("city"), d)
print(d.setdefault("country", "Pakistan"), d)
print(d.get("missing"), d.get("missing", 0))
copy_d = d.copy()
d.clear()
print(d, copy_d)

Nested Data

Real data is often a list of dictionaries (like database rows) or a dictionary that holds lists and other dictionaries.

Sets

A set holds unique values with no order. It is perfect for removing duplicates and for maths-style operations.

blocks.code:
tags = ["web", "python", "web", "css", "python"]
unique = set(tags)
print(sorted(unique), len(unique))

a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5}
print(sorted(a | b), sorted(a & b), sorted(a - b))
print(2 in a)

More About Sets

blocks.code:
s = {1, 2, 3}
s.add(4)
s.add(2)               # already there: nothing happens
s.discard(10)          # no error if missing
s.remove(1)            # error if missing
print(sorted(s))
print({1, 2} <= {1, 2, 3}, {1, 2}.isdisjoint({3, 4}))
print(sorted({1, 2, 3} ^ {3, 4}))
print(type({}), type(set()))       # {} is an empty dict, not a set!

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a missing key with d["x"] (KeyError). Use d.get("x").
  • Using a list as a dictionary key: keys must be fixed (strings, numbers, tuples).
  • Writing {} and expecting an empty set. Use set().
  • Expecting a set to keep order or to allow duplicates.

Practice Time

  1. Make a dictionary for a student (name, roll number, marks) and print each pair.
  2. Count the letters in a word and print the result as a dictionary.
  3. Given two lists of friends, print who is in both and who is only in the first.
  4. Build a phone book: ask for a name and print the number, or "not found".
  5. Group the words ["apple", "ant", "bat", "bee", "cat"] by their first letter.

Quick Summary

  • A dictionary maps unique keys to values: fast lookup by key.
  • Use get() for safe reads and items() for looping.
  • A set keeps only unique values and supports union, intersection and difference.
  • Pick the container that matches the job: list, tuple, dict or set.

Functions

Defining and Calling

A function is a named block of code you can reuse. Define it with def, send values in as parameters and send a result back with return.

blocks.code:
def square(n):
    """Return n multiplied by itself."""
    return n * n

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

print(square(7))
result = greet("Sara")
print(result)          # greet returns None

blocks.html:
• A function without return gives back None.
  • Write a short text (docstring) under def to explain what it does.
  • A function runs only when you call it: square(7).
Default, Keyword and Variable Arguments

• size=1 is a default value used when the caller does not pass one.
  • Call with names (greet(name="Ali")) for clarity.
  • *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra named ones into a dict.
Returning More Than One Value

blocks.code:
def min_max(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers)       # really returns one tuple

low, high = min_max([4, 9, 1, 7])
print(low, high)
result = min_max([1, 2])
print(result, type(result))

blocks.html: Python packs the values into a tuple and you unpack them into several variables on the left side.
Docstrings and Type Hints

blocks.code:
def area(width: float, height: float = 1.0) -> float:
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4), area(5))
print(area.__doc__)
print(area.__name__)
blocks.output:
12 5.0
Return the area of a rectangle.
area

blocks.html: Type hints (width: float, -> float) do not change how the code runs. They help you, your editor and other programmers understand what goes in and out.

Scope: local, global and nonlocal

Variables created inside a function are local: they disappear when it ends. A lambda is a tiny one-line function, often used with sorted or map.

blocks.code:
x = "global"

def show():
    x = "local"        # a different variable
    return x

print(show(), x)

counter = 0
def increase():
    global counter     # use the outside variable (avoid when you can)
    counter += 1
increase(); increase()
print(counter)

def outer():
    count = 0
    def inner():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    inner()
    return inner()
print(outer())

blocks.html: Prefer passing values in and returning results instead of using global. Functions without hidden connections are easier to test.
The Mutable Default Argument Trap

blocks.code:
def add_bad(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add_bad(1))
print(add_bad(2))      # surprise: the same list is reused

def add_good(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add_good(1))
print(add_good(2))

blocks.html: A default value is created once, when the function is defined. Never use a list or dictionary as a default; use None and create it inside.
lambda, map and filter

blocks.code:
words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w)))
print(list(map(lambda n: n * 2, [1, 2, 3])))

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
print(list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, nums)))
print(list(map(lambda n: n ** 2, nums)))
print([n ** 2 for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])     # often clearer

blocks.html: A list comprehension is usually easier to read than map and filter with a lambda. Use the one that is clearer.

Recursion

A function can call itself. Every recursive function needs a base case (when to stop) and a step that moves toward it.
Without a base case Python raises RecursionError (about 1000 calls deep). For simple counting, a loop is usually better.

Writing Good Functions

  • Give it a clear verb name: calculate_total, is_valid.
  • Make it do one job. If you write "and" in its description, split it in two.
  • Prefer return over print inside functions, so the result can be reused.
  • Keep it short: if it does not fit on one screen, think about splitting it.
  • Add a docstring that says what goes in and what comes out.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting the brackets when calling: square is the function, square(5) runs it.
  • Printing a value instead of returning it, then trying to use the result.
  • Using a list or dict as a default argument.
  • Forgetting a base case in recursion.
  • Changing a global variable inside a function without declaring it with global.

Practice Time

  1. Write is_even(n) that returns True or False.
  2. Write average(*numbers) that works for any number of values.
  3. Write celsius_to_fahrenheit(c) and use it in a loop for 0, 10, 20 ... 100.
  4. Write is_prime(n) and use it to print all primes below 50.
  5. Write a recursive function that adds the digits of a number (123 gives 6).

Quick Summary

  • def name(parameters): creates a function; return sends a value back.
  • Default values, keywords, *args and **kwargs make calls flexible.
  • Variables inside a function are local.
  • Recursion needs a base case.
  • Never use a mutable default argument.

Classes & Objects

Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing made from it. __init__ runs when an object is created, and self means "this object".

• Variables stored on self are the object's attributes.
  • Functions inside a class are methods. Their first parameter is always self.
Class Attributes vs Instance Attributes

blocks.code:
class Student:
    school = "LGU"                 # class attribute: shared by all students
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name           # instance attribute: one per object
        Student.count += 1

a, b = Student("Ayesha"), Student("Bilal")
print(a.school, b.school, Student.count)
Student.school = "Lahore Garrison University"
print(a.school)
a.name = "Aisha"
print(a.name, b.name)
blocks.output:
LGU LGU 2
Lahore Garrison University
Aisha Bilal

blocks.html: Use instance attributes for data that belongs to one object and class attributes for values shared by all objects.

Special Methods

Methods with double underscores let your class work with Python features. __str__ controls what print() shows.

MethodUsed by
__init__Creating an object
__str__ / __repr__print(obj) / the developer view
__len__len(obj)
__eq__, __lt__==, < (comparisons and sorting)
__add__The + operator

Encapsulation and Properties

Python has no strict private data. By convention, a name starting with _ means "internal, please do not touch". A property lets you control how an attribute is read or changed.

Inheritance

A class can inherit from another to reuse its code. The child can add methods or override existing ones. super() calls the parent's version.

blocks.output:
Rex says Woof
Tom says Meow

blocks.html:
Polymorphism and isinstance

Polymorphism means different classes can respond to the same method name in their own way. The loop below does not care which shape it holds.

Inheritance or Composition?

Use inheritance for an "is a" relationship (a Dog is an Animal). Use composition for a "has a" relationship (a Car has an Engine): store one object inside another.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting self as the first parameter of a method.
  • Forgetting self. before an attribute: name = name does not save anything.
  • Forgetting to call super().__init__() in a child class that has its own __init__.
  • Putting a list as a class attribute when every object needs its own list.
  • Using inheritance when composition would be simpler.

Practice Time

  1. Create a Rectangle class with area() and perimeter() methods.
  2. Create a BankAccount with deposit, withdraw and a read-only balance.
  3. Create Vehicle, then Car and Bike that inherit from it and override describe().

Quick Summary

  • A class is a blueprint, an object is an instance; self is the current object.
  • __init__ sets up attributes; other dunder methods connect to Python features.
  • _name means internal; @property controls access.
  • Inheritance reuses code; super() calls the parent; polymorphism lets subclasses differ.
  • Prefer composition when the relationship is "has a".

When something goes wrong Python raises an exception. Catch it with try and except so your program does not crash.

Custom Exceptions
A custom exception is just a class that inherits from Exception. It gives your errors a clear name.

Reading and Writing Files

Use with open(...). It closes the file for you, even if an error happens. Modes: "r" read, "w" write (erases), "a" append.

blocks.code:
import json, os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "notes.txt")

with open(path, "w") as f:          # write
    f.write("first line\n")
    f.write("second line\n")

with open(path, "a") as f:          # append
    f.write("third line\n")

with open(path) as f:               # read line by line
    for number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
        print(number, line.strip())

print(json.dumps({"name": "Ali", "scores": [90, 85]}))

try:
    open("missing.txt")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("missing.txt does not exist")

• Always handle FileNotFoundError when reading a file that may not exist.
  • Use import to use other modules, for example import json to save data as JSON.

import os, tempfile
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "data.txt")
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write("apple\nbanana\ncherry\n")

with open(path) as f:
    print(repr(f.read()))                 # the whole file as one string
with open(path) as f:
    print(f.readline().strip())           # one line
    print([line.strip() for line in f.readlines()])   # the rest as a list

Common Mistakes

  • Using "w" on a file you wanted to keep: it erases it. Use "a" to add.

  2. Write a program that saves names typed by the user into names.txt, one per line.
  3. Read names.txt and print how many lines it has and the longest name.
  4. Save a list of student dictionaries to a JSON file and load it back.

  • try / except / else / finally handle errors; catch specific exceptions.
  • raise creates an error; custom exceptions inherit from Exception.
  • Use with open(...) for files; modes are r, w, a.
  • json and csv read and write common data formats.
  • pathlib is the modern way to work with paths.

Modules, Packages & Libraries

What is a Module?

A module is just a .py file with code you can reuse. A package is a folder of modules. Python comes with a large standard library, and you can install thousands more with pip.

blocks.code:
import math
from math import sqrt, pi
import math as m

print(math.sqrt(16), sqrt(25), round(pi, 4), m.floor(3.7), m.ceil(3.2))
print(math.pow(2, 3), math.factorial(5), math.gcd(12, 18))

blocks.html:
StyleExampleUse it as
Import the moduleimport mathmath.sqrt(9)
Import namesfrom math import sqrtsqrt(9)
Import with a short nameimport numpy as npnp.array([1, 2])

Avoid from module import *: it pollutes your names and makes the code hard to read.

from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

d = date(2026, 11, 20)

blocks.html: date.today() and datetime.now() give the current date and time. Use strftime to choose the format and strptime to read dates from text.

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque

print(Counter("mississippi").most_common(2))     # counting made easy

groups = defaultdict(list)                        # missing keys start as []
for word in ["apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry"]:
    groups[word[0]].append(word)
print(dict(groups))

queue = deque([1, 2, 3])                          # fast at both ends
queue.append(4)
print(queue.popleft(), queue)

blocks.html:
Making Your Own Module

Save this as mytools.py:

def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(greet("test"))     # runs only when this file is run directly

Then use it from another file in the same folder:

import mytools
print(mytools.greet("Sara"))

blocks.output:
__main__
This file is being run directly

blocks.html: When a file is run, Python sets __name__ to "__main__". When it is imported, __name__ is the module name. The if __name__ == "__main__": guard keeps test code from running on import.

pip and Virtual Environments

pip installs libraries from the Python Package Index (PyPI). Use a virtual environment so each project has its own libraries.

python -m venv venv                 # create the environment
venv\Scripts\activate               # Windows
source venv/bin/activate            # macOS / Linux

pip install requests                # install a library
pip list                            # see what is installed
pip freeze > requirements.txt       # save the list
pip install -r requirements.txt     # install from the list later

Commit requirements.txt to Git, but do not commit the venv folder.

Example with the popular requests library (needs internet, so it is shown here but not run):

import requests

response = requests.get("https://api.github.com")
print(response.status_code)           # 200 means OK
print(response.json()["current_user_url"])

Common Mistakes

  • Naming your file like a module you import (random.py, math.py): Python imports your file instead.
  • ModuleNotFoundError: the library is not installed in the active environment. Run pip install.
  • Installing libraries globally for every project instead of using a virtual environment.
  • Circular imports: file A imports B and B imports A. Move shared code to a third file.

  1. Use random to build a number-guessing game (guess between 1 and 20, with hints).
  2. Use datetime to print how many days are left until your next exam.
  3. Use collections.Counter to find the three most common words in a paragraph.
  4. Make mytools.py with three functions and import it from another file.
  5. Create a virtual environment, install requests and print the status code of a website.

Quick Summary

  • A module is a .py file; a package is a folder of modules.
  • Import with import x, from x import y or import x as z.
  • The standard library is huge: math, random, datetime, collections, json, os.
  • pip installs outside libraries; use a virtual environment per project.
  • if __name__ == "__main__": separates "run" from "import".

Next Level Python

Comprehensions in Depth

blocks.code:
nums = range(1, 11)
print([n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])               # list
print({n: n ** 2 for n in range(4)})                      # dict
print({len(w) for w in ["a", "bb", "cc", "ddd"]})         # set
print([(x, y) for x in range(2) for y in "ab"])           # nested loops
print(["even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd" for n in range(4)])

blocks.html: A comprehension is great for short, simple transformations. If it needs several conditions or becomes hard to read, use a normal for loop.

Iterators and Generators

A generator produces values one at a time with yield, so it never has to hold everything in memory. Perfect for big files or endless sequences.

Decorators

A decorator wraps a function to add behaviour (logging, timing, checking permissions) without changing the function itself. You apply it with @name.
@shout above def add is the same as writing add = shout(add). Frameworks such as Flask use decorators for routes: @app.route("/").

Context Managers

The with statement runs setup and cleanup code automatically. Files use it, and you can write your own.

dataclasses and Type Hints

A dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you. It is ideal for classes that mainly store data.
Type hints are not enforced when the program runs, but tools such as mypy and editors like VS Code use them to catch mistakes early.
Unpacking Tricks
* spreads a list or tuple, ** spreads a dictionary. They also work when building new lists and dictionaries.
